summaries.example: Imagine water in a cup and water in a bottle. We can talk about each portion, or about all the water together. But we usually do not say “one water” and “two waters” unless we mean two servings or kinds. This shows why language treats water differently from countable things such as cups.
summaries.summary: The entry studies mass expressions: words such as water, gold, furniture, and wisdom. These words are contrasted with count expressions such as rabbit, bottle, and idea. One important difference is grammatical. Count expressions usually have singular and plural forms and can go with one, two, or many. Mass expressions usually go with much or a lot of and do not normally show singular and plural in the same way. However, a word can sometimes be used in either way, so the difference may depend on how the word is used in a sentence. The entry also asks what mass expressions mean. A tempting answer is that every part of a mass thing is also that thing, but this fails: a table is furniture, while a leg of the table is not necessarily furniture, and oxygen is not water even though water contains oxygen. The entry therefore examines different logical tools for describing portions, sums, sets, measurement, and ways a sentence can be understood.
key_ideas: Mass expressions often behave differently from count expressions. We say “much water” but “many cups.”
Some words can be used in both ways. We might say “two waters” when we mean two glasses or servings.
The source argues that grammar is a better guide than meaning alone for telling mass and count uses apart.
Several theories try to explain how sentences about substances work, but each theory has difficult cases.
Mass expressions can describe one whole amount or several related portions, depending on the situation.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use mass expressions every day, but their grammar and meaning are surprisingly complex. Understanding them helps explain why sentences about water, furniture, gold, or wisdom do not work exactly like sentences about cats or chairs. It also shows how philosophers and language researchers test theories: a good theory should handle ordinary examples, unusual cases, and connections between different kinds of sentences.

important_terms.definition: A word used for something treated as a substance, material, or idea rather than as separate countable objects, such as water, furniture, or wisdom.
A word that normally can have a singular form and a plural form, such as cat and cats or idea and ideas.
The way words are put together in a sentence, including which words can go with them, such as much, many, one, or two.
The idea that separate portions can be joined and still be called by the same mass word. Water in two cups can together be water.

questions_to_think_about: Why do we say “much rice” but “many bowls”?
Can you think of a word that can be used as both a mass expression and a count expression?
If half of a table is furniture, is every tiny part of that table furniture?
When someone says “the fruit costs ten dollars,” do they mean all the fruit together or each group of fruit?

summaries.example: Suppose two pieces of gold exist, a and b, and only a is in a safe. What should “The gold is in the safe” and “The gold is not in the safe” mean? A simple theory that treats “the gold” as the sum a+b may make both sentences false, because the whole amount is neither entirely in the safe nor entirely outside it. This illustrates why negation and part-structure complicate the logic of mass expressions.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates the logic and semantics of mass expressions, including concrete terms such as water and furniture and abstract terms such as wisdom and love. It first considers how mass expressions differ from count expressions. Syntactic tests appeal to number marking and determiners: count expressions typically allow singular/plural contrast and numerals, while mass expressions combine naturally with much or a little. Since expressions can shift uses, some researchers place the distinction at the noun-phrase level rather than in the noun. The entry concludes that syntactic criteria are satisfactory, whereas no necessary and sufficient semantic definition appears to cover all cases across languages. Cumulative reference is compatible with mass expressions but also with plurals. Distributive reference is too strong: parts of water or furniture need not themselves be water or furniture. Several semantic frameworks follow. A mereological approach uses sums and parthood; a set-theoretic approach uses membership; a mixed approach combines a set of portions organized by sums or joins with ordinary set-theoretic interpretation. The mixed approach improves the treatment of definite descriptions and identity across time, but negation creates cases in which a whole amount is partly related to a predicate and partly not. Boolean complement or non-overlap can help in homogeneous cases, yet they fail for vague or additive predicates such as cheap or costs fifty euros. The entry also examines quantifiers, context-sensitive measures, collective and non-collective readings, coverings, non-singular reference, and abstract mass nouns. Overall, it presents competing proposals and the precise problems each must address rather than declaring one final solution.
key_ideas: The mass/count distinction may be located in nouns themselves or in the noun phrases formed in context. The entry adopts the traditional noun-level view for discussion, while recognizing the competing position.
Syntactic evidence is more reliable than proposed semantic definitions. Cumulative reference also occurs with plural count expressions, and distributive reference fails for many mass nouns.
A purely mereological theory represents mass nouns with sums and predication with parthood, but it faces minimal-part and uniformity problems.
A purely set-theoretic theory represents mass nouns as sets, but it must explain which portions belong in those sets and how definite descriptions work over time.
A mixed theory combines set membership with sums or joins. It handles several problems, yet negation remains difficult, especially when only part of an amount satisfies a predicate.
Quantifiers such as some, all, little, much, and most can be analyzed using intersection and, for quantity, a context-sensitive measure function. Interpretations may be absolute or proportional.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mass expressions connect ordinary grammar with difficult questions about parts, wholes, sets, quantities, identity, and truth. A satisfactory account should explain why “some wine” can refer to a portion, why “the wine” can refer to a combined amount, why a part of furniture need not be furniture, and why negated sentences can be sensitive to how an object is divided. The topic also matters cross-linguistically: a word treated as mass in one language may be count in another, and languages without ordinary singular/plural marking may organize nouns differently. Studying these cases reveals how formal logic can clarify language while also showing where simple models break down.

important_terms.definition: A linguistic category involving nouns or noun phrases that present material, substance, or abstract content without ordinary singular/plural counting, as in water, furniture, or wisdom.
A linguistic category involving items that normally permit singular/plural contrast and combine with numerals or count determiners, as in table/tables.
The study of how expressions are structured and what grammatical environments they can enter.
A proposed meaning-based property. Cumulative reference allows separate portions satisfying a mass noun to be combined while still satisfying it.
A proposed property according to which a thing satisfying a predicate would have all of its parts satisfy it. The entry argues that this is not true of all mass nouns.
A theory of parts and wholes. A mereological sum combines portions, and parthood relates a portion to a larger whole.
A formal system using sets, membership, intersection, and related operations to represent meanings and truth conditions.
An interpretation in which a mass noun phrase is understood as applying to an entire amount together, rather than separately to each relevant portion.

questions_to_think_about: If a mass noun can be used countably in one context and massively in another, is the distinction best assigned to the noun or to the whole noun phrase?
Why does the failure of distributive reference matter for examples involving furniture or water?
Should “The gold is not in the safe” be true when some gold is in the safe and some is outside? What would each answer predict?
How might a measure function distinguish “much gold was stolen” as a large amount from the claim that a large proportion of the gold was stolen?
Does a theory that uses non-singular terms offer a better account of mass expressions that refer to one or several things at once?

summaries.example: At a snack table, there is juice in three cups. You might say, “There is some juice on the table,” referring to one or more portions together. But you usually say “three cups,” not “three juices.” If you say “two juices,” you may mean two servings. The word juice has shifted into a count use because of the sentence and situation.
summaries.summary: This entry asks how language handles mass expressions such as water, gold, furniture, wisdom, and love. Count expressions usually allow singular and plural forms: one rabbit, two rabbits. Mass expressions usually do not work that way and instead combine with words such as much, little, or a lot of. Yet this difference is not completely fixed. A mass expression can be used as a count expression in a suitable context, and a count expression can sometimes be used in a mass-like way. Because of this flexibility, some researchers say the mass/count distinction belongs to noun phrases rather than nouns. The entry favors syntactic tests over attempts to define mass expressions by meaning alone. One proposed meaning is cumulative reference: if two separate portions are water, their combined amount is also water. But plural count expressions have this property too. Another proposal, distributive reference, says that every part of something called furniture or water must also be furniture or water. That does not work generally, since a table leg is not necessarily furniture and oxygen is not water. The entry then compares theories. Mereology explains mass expressions through sums and parts. Set theory explains them through sets and membership. A mixed approach uses both: portions form an organized collection of sums, while ordinary predication uses set relations. This helps with descriptions and amounts, but negation remains difficult when only part of a whole satisfies a description. The entry also discusses quantifiers, different ways of understanding collective statements, coverings, reference to one or several things, and abstract mass expressions such as love and wisdom.
key_ideas: Mass and count expressions differ in grammar: “much juice” contrasts with “many cups,” and “one idea” contrasts with “one wisdom.”
The same noun may be used in different ways. This supports the view that the distinction can depend on the noun phrase and its grammatical setting.
Meaning-based tests are less dependable. Joining portions works for mass expressions, but it also works for plural count expressions.
A theory based only on parts and wholes has trouble with parts that do not count as the same material, such as a table leg and furniture.
A theory based only on sets has trouble deciding which portions a phrase like “the clay on the desk” refers to. A mixed theory combines sets with sums.
Negation and quantifiers reveal further problems. Context can affect whether “much” means a large amount or a large share, and whether a sentence concerns a whole amount or separate groups.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mass expressions are part of ordinary speech, but they expose hidden choices about counting, dividing, combining, and describing things. Learning about them helps explain why grammar cannot always be predicted from everyday meaning. It also introduces a central philosophical method: compare possible theories, find the examples that challenge them, and keep the parts that work while revising the parts that fail. The same issues appear in language about substances, groups, abstract qualities, and objects that change over time.

important_terms.definition: An expression for material or abstract content viewed as an amount or substance, such as juice, gold, furniture, or wisdom.
An expression that normally names separate items and can take singular and plural forms, such as cup/cups or idea/ideas.
The grammatical pattern that determines which forms and neighboring words an expression can have.
A property in which separate things that are each called by a mass word can be joined and still be called by that word.
A proposed property saying that if a whole is described by a word, its parts are also described by that word. The entry explains why this does not fit all mass expressions.
A way to study parts and wholes. A sum is a larger whole made from portions, and parthood says that one thing is included in another.
An approach that represents meanings with sets and explains predication through membership or overlap between sets.
A reading in which a phrase applies to an amount as a whole. A non-collective reading applies it to relevant groups or portions instead.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “two waters” be understandable even though water is usually treated as a mass expression?
Does combining two portions always produce something that should be described by the same word?
If some of a pile of gold is in a box and the rest is outside, is “the gold is in the box” true, false, or unclear?
What is the difference between saying that much of the juice was spilled and saying that much of the juice in one particular cup was spilled?
Can a phrase describe several objects at once without turning into an ordinary plural expression?
